bib.title: Natural Language Processing with Python, Chapter 4: Writing Structured Programs

question: How can one write well-structured, readable, reusable Python programs for language processing, and avoid common pitfalls in assignment, functions and algorithm design?
contributions: Consolidates Python fundamentals (assignment and references, sequences, functions, modules, debugging) with NLP examples
Introduces algorithm-design ideas used in NLP: recursion, space-time trade-offs, dynamic programming
Surveys Matplotlib, NetworkX, csv and NumPy for language data

limits: Written for Python 2.5/2.6 and NLTK 2.0 (2009): print statements, cmp, izip, basestring, raw_input, FreqDist.inc and FreqDist.keys() sorted by frequency, nltk.clean_url, nltk.memoize, nltk.defaultdict, nltk.Index and nltk.edit_dist as used no longer work as printed in Python 3 / NLTK 3.

The text says the chapter follows language structure rather than NLP needs, so only parts bear on NLP: generator expressions and generator functions for streaming, enumerate/zip, n-gram sliding windows, set versus list vocabulary lookup, integer-id vocabularies, word-frequency tables, dynamic programming and memoisation, tries, sorting with a key.
Timings are single runs on an unstated machine and Python version; the 50% hit rate statement may be wrong because of operator precedence in the printed statement.

No text-wrapping or justification content except exercise 31; sorting appears as sort(), sorted(), a key/cmp argument and the divide-and-conquer merge sort illustration, not as an algorithmic treatment.
No evaluation of NLP methods, no models, no training: pure programming pedagogy.
practices: Use declarative built-ins (sum, max, sorted(set(tokens)), enumerate) rather than manual counters and loop variables (Section 4.3).
Use generator expressions and yield-based generators when the consumer only needs a stream, to avoid building large lists (Sections 4.2, 4.5).
Build 2-D structures of sets or lists with nested comprehensions, never with list multiplication, because multiplication copies references (Sections 4.1, 4.3).
Copy with foo[:] for one level and copy.deepcopy for nested structures (Section 4.1).
A function should either modify its argument or return a value, not both (Section 4.4, my_sort1/2/3).
Do not use a mutable object as a default parameter value (Sections 4.5, 4.6).
Avoid global declarations; pass inputs as parameters and return outputs (Section 4.4).
Check argument types with assert isinstance(...) rather than returning None (Section 4.4).
Break code longer than 10-20 lines into functions with a one-sentence docstring; docstring may hold a doctest (Section 4.4).
Store a vocabulary as a set, not a list, for membership tests (Section 4.7).
Replace tokens by integer ids with a word-to-id dictionary before language modelling (Example 4-8, Section 4.7).
Use dynamic programming or memoisation when subproblems overlap (Section 4.7).
When debugging, shrink the input, add prints, use pdb, and treat each fix as a hypothesis; keep doctest regression tests (Section 4.6).
Prefer iteration over recursion for speed since recursion pushes stack frames; use recursion when it is clearer, e.g. nested hierarchies and tries (Section 4.7).
Use rsplit('.', 2) rather than split('.') for WordNet synset names such as ph.d..n.01 (Section 4.6).

terms.definition: the value of a structured object such as a list is just a reference to the object, so assignment copies the reference
is tests object identity, == tests equivalence; parallels the type-token distinction
typically a fixed-length collection of objects of different types whose meaning depends on position; immutable, unlike a list
a comprehension without brackets that streams values to the calling function instead of building a list
procedural dictates machine operations step by step; declarative uses high-level built-ins and leaves implementation to the interpreter
function parameters are values, but the value of a structured object is a reference to it
name resolution looks at local, then global, then built-in names
attack a problem of size n by dividing it into two problems of size n/2, solve them and combine the results (merge sort, binary search)
a function that simplifies the problem and calls itself on one or more easier instances, then combines the results
a nested dictionary indexing a lexicon one letter at a time, built recursively

a technique for problems with overlapping subproblems: store each subproblem solution in a lookup table instead of recomputing it; bottom-up fills the table from small to large, top-down is recursive with a stored-result check
storing the result of each call along with its parameters and returning the stored result on repeat calls

figures.caption: List assignment and computer memory: Two list objects foo and bar reference the same location in the computer's memory; updating foo will also modify bar, and vice versa.

Sorting by divide-and-conquer: To sort an array, we split it in half and sort each half (recursively); we merge each sorted half back into a whole list (again recursively); this algorithm is known as Merge Sort.
